abstract: A Lean 4 development of Kuhn's simplified two-person poker (Kuhn 1950): three cards 1 < 2 < 3, one dealt to each player with the six deals equiprobable, an ante of a from each player and a single bet of b, player I acting first, the five courses of play of Kuhn's p. 98 with payoffs a (pass-pass, to the higher card), a to II (pass-bet-pass), a + b to the higher card (pass-bet-bet), a to I (bet-pass) and a + b to the higher card (bet-bet). The definitions are built from the game tree: a behaviour strategy of I is a pair of functions on the three cards (the probability of betting first, the probability of calling after passing and facing a bet), one of II likewise (the probability of betting after a pass, the probability of calling a bet); the payoff is the average over the six deals; a strategy guarantees v when it is valid and earns at least v (holds the opponent to at most v) against every valid strategy of the opponent; the game has value v when each player has a strategy guaranteeing v; an equilibrium is a saddle point. For Kuhn's game a = b = 1, kernel-checked: the value is -1/18 (a game has at most one value), an equilibrium exists, every equilibrium pays I exactly -1/18, and a pair is an equilibrium iff each strategy guarantees -1/18; II's optimal strategy is unique at all six information sets (bet after a pass with the 1, 2, 3 with probabilities 1/3, 0, 1; call with probabilities 0, 1/3, 1 - Kuhn's (xi, eta) = (1/3, 1/3) with the four coordinates he removed as superfluous now proved forced); I's optimal strategies are exactly Kuhn's one-parameter family (bet the 1 with probability alpha and fold it, never bet the 2 first and call with it with probability alpha + 1/3, bet the 3 with probability 3 alpha and call with it, for alpha in [0, 1/3], the call with the 3 being unconstrained exactly when 3 alpha = 1, where that information set is unreached); in the normal form with Kuhn's coding of the 27 and 64 pure strategies, his essential 8 x 4 matrix is six times the game matrix, his twelve basic optimal mixed strategies (A)-(L) and II's two guarantee -1/18, and a mixed strategy is optimal iff its realization plan lies on the family (I) or its marginals are II's strategy (II). For every ante a > 0 and bet b > 0 (Kuhn's pp. 102-103, stated there without proof, and the region b > 2a he does not state): the value is -b^2/(6(2a + b)) for b <= a, -b(2a - b)/(6(2a + b)) for a <= b <= 2a and 0 for b >= 2a, with explicit guaranteeing strategies in each case; in Case 3 the calling probability eta with the 2 ranges over [(2a - b)/(2a + b), b/(2a + b)], and the interval printed on p. 102, b/(2a + b) <= eta <= (a + b)/(2a + b), fails at its upper end (at a = 2, b = 3 and eta = 5/7 II's Case 3 strategy does not guarantee the value). Every guarantee is a finite nonnegative-product identity (the gap between the payoff and the value is a sum of products of the opponent's probabilities and their complements with coefficients nonnegative on the case's region: polynomials in a, b and the free parameter, at general stakes built from a, b, 2a + b, a - b, 2a - b, 4a - b, b - 2a and the interval factors (2a + b)eta - (2a - b), b - (2a + b)eta, 2(a - b) - (2a + b)xi, and, in the optimal-set theorems, the slacks of their stated inequalities), and every "only if" is a linear certificate from finitely many pure strategies (the coefficients rationals at a = b = 1 and, at general stakes, polynomials in a, b and the free parameter nonnegative on the case's region); no formal library found by the dated search holds the game. Beyond Kuhn's statements: the two certificate identities are stated as theorems; the equilibria of Kuhn's game are exactly the pairs (kuhnI α k, kuhnII) with α in [0, 1/3], k in [0, 1] and 3α = 1 or k = 1; and at general stakes the optimal sets are determined - I's strategy is unique for b < a (up to the unreached call with the 3) and for a < b <= 2a, is Kuhn's family on the diagonal b = a at every scale, and for b >= 2a never bets the 1 or the 2 first, folds them, and with the 3 is cut out by one inequality (a single strategy at b = 2a; beyond it a two-dimensional set in which I may also bet the 3 first, with probability at most (b - 2a)/b), so Kuhn's one-parameter family is optimal only at b = a; II's strategy is unique on the diagonal at every scale and a segment for b <= a (the bet with the 2 after a pass free in [0, 2(a - b)/(2a + b)], so Kuhn's 'unique optimal mode of behavior' in Case 1 holds in his behaviour parameters only); for a <= b < 2a its bets after a pass are forced, (b/(2a + b), 0, 1), and its calls form a polytope of three inequalities; for b > 2a it never bets the 1 or the 2 after a pass, never calls with them, and calls with the 3 with probability at least 4a/(2a + b), its bet with the 3 free; and on the line b = 2a its optimal set is a five-dimensional polytope (the bet with the 2 after a pass zero and, with bets (p, 0, r) and calls (s, t, w), 2p <= r, s + t <= p, 1 <= t + w, 1 + p + s <= 2w; nine vertices, replayed); at every ante a > 0 and bet b > 0 every equilibrium pays the value and a pair is an equilibrium iff each strategy guarantees it, so the equilibria are exactly the pairs of optimal strategies, on b = 2a explicitly; the corrected Case 3 interval is sharp, and the printed one holds only at its lower end. A second correction, a misprint, is noted in the documentation: p. 101's table gives β = 5/12 for (I) and (J), where p. 100's mixtures and p. 101's own formula give 7/12.

related_formalizations.note: minimax-theorem-lean (Arthur742Ramos, registered 2026-10-01): for every finite two-player zero-sum game, the sup-inf and inf-sup of the expected payoff over mixed strategies agree (von Neumann's minimax theorem; its three definitions are comparator holes, which the repository defines so, proving a saddle point through Mathlib's Sion theorem). Its theorem implies that Kuhn poker's 27 x 64 normal form has a value; it does not compute it. This entry exhibits the value and both optimal sets directly, by certificates, in behaviour and in mixed strategies, and shares no code with it.

Verified regret matching and finite-time equilibrium computation (Arthur742Ramos, registered 2026-09-08): regret bounds and approximate equilibria of finite zero-sum matrix games by self-play; its repository metadata states that no extensive-form or poker performance theorem is claimed. Kuhn poker is a standard test game in that literature; no equilibrium of it is stated there. No code is shared.

A Lean 4 game-theory library (extensive-form games, behaviour strategies and perfect recall after Kuhn 1953, counterfactual-regret modules; main at e33b131, 2026-10-09, read by tree path and content search, and re-read 2026-10-10 with no poker path on main or on the branch pushed that day). It holds no poker instance and no value of Kuhn poker. No code is shared; this entry builds its game from the tree without a library.

title: Kuhn poker: the value −1/18, all optimal strategies, and the solution at every ante and bet
